star-positions.title: The Positions of the Stars
star-positions.hook: An oath by “the positions of the stars”, called great “if you only knew”. Astronomers found that no star is quite where it seems.
star-positions.word.0: by the positions, the places where they fall
star-positions.science.0: The stars look fixed. But in 1718 Edmond Halley showed that Sirius, Arcturus and Aldebaran had moved more than half a degree since the Greek astronomer Hipparchus charted them, some 1,850 years earlier.
star-positions.science.1: In 1727 James Bradley explained why every star seems to shift back and forth over a year, by up to about 20 arcseconds: light travels at a finite speed while the Earth moves around the Sun. Because light takes time, we also see each star where it was when its light set out, years or thousands of years ago.
star-positions.science.2: In 1838 Friedrich Bessel measured the first distance to a star, 61 Cygni. The Gaia space telescope (2013–2025) has since measured the positions and motions of more than a billion stars.
star-positions.stats.0.label: Halley shows the “fixed” stars move
star-positions.stats.1.label: Yearly shift of every star (aberration)
star-positions.stats.2.label: Stars in Gaia's 2018 map
star-positions.proof.0.title: Halley: the fixed stars move
star-positions.proof.0.text: Edmond Halley compares his star positions with the ancient catalogue of Hipparchus and finds Sirius, Arcturus and Aldebaran displaced by more than half a degree.
star-positions.proof.1.title: Bradley: aberration
star-positions.proof.1.text: James Bradley explains a yearly back-and-forth shift in star positions: light's finite speed combined with the Earth's motion tilts where stars appear.
star-positions.proof.2.title: Bessel: the first distance to a star
star-positions.proof.2.text: Friedrich Bessel measures the parallax of 61 Cygni, the first reliable distance to a star.
star-positions.proof.3.title: Gaia
star-positions.proof.3.text: ESA's Gaia space telescope maps the positions, distances and motions of more than a billion stars.
star-positions.fit.0: Mawāqiʿ means the places where things fall or are set. Astronomers found that the positions we see are shifted by motion and by the time light takes to arrive.
star-positions.fit.1: The verse calls the oath great “if you only knew”, hinting there is more to the stars' positions than meets the eye.
star-positions.gap.0: Classical commentators read mawāqiʿ as the places where the stars set, or their stations in the sky. Some early commentators read nujūm as the parts in which the Quran was revealed.
star-positions.gap.1: The verse does not mention motion, light or distance. The link rests on the reading of one word.
star-positions.media.0.cap: Gaia's map of our galaxy, built from measurements of nearly 1.7 billion stars (ESA).
star-positions.media.1.cap: James Bradley, who discovered the aberration of starlight.
star-positions.media.2.cap: Friedrich Bessel, who measured the first distance to a star.
smaller-than-atom.title: Smaller Than an Atom's Weight
smaller-than-atom.hook: “Not an atom's weight… nor anything smaller than that.” The Greek word atom means “uncuttable”, until physics found smaller things inside it.
smaller-than-atom.word.1: a speck, a tiny ant (today: an atom)
smaller-than-atom.science.0: Greek thinkers such as Democritus imagined that matter is made of tiny “atoms”, a word that means “uncuttable”. When John Dalton revived the idea in the early 1800s, atoms were still thought to be the smallest units of matter.
smaller-than-atom.science.1: Then they were cut. In 1897 J. J. Thomson discovered the electron, far lighter than any atom. In 1911 Ernest Rutherford showed that nearly all of an atom's mass sits in a nucleus about 27,000 to 60,000 times narrower than the atom itself. The proton was named in 1920 and the neutron was discovered in 1932.
smaller-than-atom.science.2: In 1968 experiments at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center showed that protons themselves contain smaller, point-like particles, now called quarks.
smaller-than-atom.stats.0.label: The electron: first particle smaller than an atom
smaller-than-atom.stats.1.label: How much narrower the nucleus is than the atom
smaller-than-atom.stats.2.label: Quarks seen inside the proton
smaller-than-atom.proof.0.title: Thomson: the electron
smaller-than-atom.proof.0.text: J. J. Thomson shows that cathode rays are streams of particles much lighter than any atom: the first thing found to be smaller.
smaller-than-atom.proof.1.title: Rutherford: the nucleus
smaller-than-atom.proof.1.text: Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden fire alpha particles at gold foil and a few bounce straight back. Rutherford concludes that the atom's mass sits in a tiny nucleus.
smaller-than-atom.proof.1.cap: Expected and observed results of the gold foil experiment.
smaller-than-atom.proof.2.title: Chadwick: the neutron
smaller-than-atom.proof.2.text: James Chadwick discovers the neutron, a particle distinct from the proton, completing the picture of the nucleus.
smaller-than-atom.proof.3.title: SLAC: quarks
smaller-than-atom.proof.3.text: Electrons fired at protons at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center bounce off smaller, point-like particles inside them: quarks.
smaller-than-atom.fit.0: The verses name the dharra and then go further, to “anything smaller than that”. Matter turned out to have smaller and smaller parts.
smaller-than-atom.fit.1: The phrase appears in more than one verse (10:61 and 34:3), always stressing that nothing is too small for God's knowledge.
smaller-than-atom.gap.0: In classical Arabic, dharra meant a tiny ant or a speck of dust in a sunbeam. It came to mean “atom” later, so early readers did not hear a physics claim.
smaller-than-atom.gap.1: The verses are about God's knowledge, not the structure of matter. “Smaller than that” says only that nothing is too small to be known.
smaller-than-atom.gap.2: Ideas about the smallest particles are much older than Islam, in Greek and Indian philosophy, and Muslim theologians debated atoms too.
smaller-than-atom.media.0.cap: The track of an atomic nucleus from space, caught in a cloud chamber (1960).
smaller-than-atom.media.1.cap: Rutherford's result: most particles pass straight through, a few bounce off a tiny nucleus.
sea-fire.title: The Sea Set Aflame
sea-fire.hook: An oath “by the sea set aflame”. In 1977 scientists found hot springs on the ocean floor; some vent water hotter than 400 °C.
sea-fire.word.1: are set aflame, made to overflow
sea-fire.science.0: Along the mid-ocean ridges, a chain of undersea mountains 65,000 km long, the Earth's crust is pulling apart and hot rock rises close to the seafloor. In February 1977 geologists diving in the submersible Alvin found warm springs on the Galápagos Rift, surrounded by giant tube worms, clams and whole communities living in total darkness.
sea-fire.science.1: In April 1979, on the East Pacific Rise, Alvin found chimneys jetting black, mineral-laden water: the first “black smokers”. Vent water can be hotter than 400 °C, and a brief 464 °C has been measured. It does not boil because of the crushing pressure of the deep. Lava erupts on the seafloor along the ridges as well.
sea-fire.stats.0.label: First vents found, Galápagos Rift
sea-fire.stats.1.label: First black smokers, East Pacific Rise
sea-fire.stats.2.label: Hottest vent water measured
sea-fire.disc.who: Corliss & van Andel · Spiess, Macdonald et al. (Alvin)
sea-fire.proof.0.title: First signs
sea-fire.proof.0.text: A Scripps Institution of Oceanography expedition towing cameras over the Galápagos Rift finds the first evidence of hot springs on the seafloor.
sea-fire.proof.1.title: Vents full of life
sea-fire.proof.1.text: On 17 February 1977 Jack Corliss and Tjeerd van Andel dive in Alvin and see the vents and the life around them (Science 203, 1073).
sea-fire.proof.2.title: Black smokers
sea-fire.proof.2.text: On 21 April 1979, on the East Pacific Rise at 21° N, William Normark and Thierry Juteau find chimneys jetting black particles. A temperature probe is rigged to measure how hot they are (Science 207, 1421).
sea-fire.proof.3.title: Loki's Castle
sea-fire.proof.3.text: Scientists from the University of Bergen find black smokers at 73° N, between Greenland and Norway: the most northerly known.
sea-fire.fit.0: Masjūr and sujjirat come from a root used for firing an oven. Beneath the sea there are vents of scalding water and erupting lava.
sea-fire.fit.1: The vents lie under kilometres of dark water and were unknown until 1977.
sea-fire.gap.0: Classical commentators give several meanings: “filled”, “held back”, or “set on fire on the Last Day”. 81:6 describes the end of the world.
sea-fire.gap.1: There are no flames under the sea. Vent water is scalding but does not burn, and lava cools almost at once.
sea-fire.gap.2: Volcanic islands erupting from the sea were seen long before, for example Thera in the Aegean.
sea-fire.media.0.cap: A black smoker on a mid-ocean ridge in the Atlantic (NOAA).
sea-fire.media.1.cap: A 255 °C vent near the top of a 38-metre sulfide chimney in the Pacific (NOAA).
sea-fire.media.2.cap: The submersible Alvin in 1978, a year after it found the first vents.
earth-quivers.title: The Earth Stirs When Rain Falls
earth-quivers.hook: “You see the earth stilled; then when We send down rain on it, it stirs and swells.” Soil scientists have measured both.
earth-quivers.science.0: When rain falls on dry ground, the ground really moves. Clay soils soak up water and swell, lifting the surface, and seeds drink water and swell before they sprout.
earth-quivers.science.1: Life in the soil wakes up too. In 1958 H. F. Birch showed that wetting dried soil sets off a sudden burst of microbial activity, releasing carbon dioxide and nitrogen. Soil scientists now call it the Birch effect.
earth-quivers.science.2: In 2015 Youngsoo Joung and Cullen Buie filmed raindrops hitting soil at high speed: each drop traps tiny bubbles of air that burst out of the ground as a fine mist of aerosols. The smell of rain on dry earth was named petrichor by Isabel Bear and Richard Thomas in 1964.
earth-quivers.stats.0.label: The Birch effect described
earth-quivers.stats.1.label: Petrichor named
earth-quivers.stats.2.label: Raindrop aerosols filmed
earth-quivers.disc.who: H. F. Birch · Bear & Thomas · Joung & Buie
earth-quivers.proof.0.title: Birch: the soil wakes up
earth-quivers.proof.0.text: H. F. Birch finds that when dried soil is wetted again, its microbes release a burst of carbon dioxide and nitrogen (Plant and Soil 10, 9).
earth-quivers.proof.1.title: Petrichor
earth-quivers.proof.1.text: Isabel Bear and Richard Thomas of Australia's CSIRO extract the oily source of the smell of rain from dry rocks and soil, and name it petrichor (Nature 201, 993).
earth-quivers.proof.2.title: Raindrops filmed
earth-quivers.proof.2.text: Youngsoo Joung and Cullen Buie at MIT film raindrops landing on soils at high speed. The drops release aerosols from the ground (Nature Communications 6, 6083).
earth-quivers.fit.0: Ihtazzat (it stirs) and rabat (it swells) describe what rain does to dry ground: it swells, gives off gas and bursts into life.
earth-quivers.fit.1: The verse compares this to bringing the dead back to life, and dry soil does come alive with microbes and seedlings.
earth-quivers.gap.0: Anyone who watched rain fall on dry land saw it soften, swell and turn green. The first listeners did not need a microscope.
earth-quivers.gap.1: Classical commentators read the words as the earth moving with sprouting plants and swelling with growth.
earth-quivers.gap.2: The Birch effect and raindrop aerosols are modern details that the verse does not mention.
earth-quivers.media.0.cap: A single raindrop hitting the soil (USDA).
altitude-breath.title: Breathless, as if Climbing Into the Sky
altitude-breath.hook: A heart closed to guidance feels “tight and constricted, as though climbing into the sky”. The higher you climb, the less air there is to breathe.
altitude-breath.science.0: Air has weight. Evangelista Torricelli made the first barometer in 1643, and in 1648 Florin Périer, at Blaise Pascal's urging, carried one up the Puy de Dôme in France. The higher he climbed, the lower the mercury stood: the air thins with height.
altitude-breath.science.1: In 1878 Paul Bert showed that the harm of altitude comes from the low pressure of oxygen. At 5,000 metres the air pressure is about half its sea-level value, and at the top of Mount Everest only about a third. Breathing speeds up and the chest labours; above 5,500 metres, which doctors call extreme altitude, blood oxygen falls sharply.
altitude-breath.stats.0.label: Air pressure falls with height (Pascal & Périer)
altitude-breath.stats.1.label: Air pressure at 5,000 m, compared with sea level
altitude-breath.stats.2.label: Air pressure on the summit of Everest
altitude-breath.proof.0.title: Torricelli's barometer
altitude-breath.proof.0.text: Evangelista Torricelli balances a column of mercury against the weight of the air: the first barometer.
altitude-breath.proof.1.title: Up the Puy de Dôme
altitude-breath.proof.1.text: Florin Périer, urged by his brother-in-law Blaise Pascal, measures the mercury at three heights on the mountain. The higher he goes, the lower it stands.
altitude-breath.proof.1.cap: An engraving of the Puy de Dôme experiment.
altitude-breath.proof.2.title: Bert: it is the oxygen
altitude-breath.proof.2.text: Paul Bert's La Pression barométrique shows that the harm of altitude comes from the low pressure of oxygen.
altitude-breath.proof.3.title: Measured on Everest
altitude-breath.proof.3.text: Members of the American Medical Research Expedition to Everest measure the air pressure on the summit (West et al., J. Appl. Physiol. 1983).
altitude-breath.fit.0: Yaṣṣaʿʿadu describes climbing with great effort, and a tight, constricted chest is how climbing into thin air feels.
altitude-breath.fit.1: The comparison points upward, “into the sky”, where the air does grow thinner.
altitude-breath.gap.0: The verse is a simile for a heart closed to faith, not a statement about air pressure.
altitude-breath.gap.1: People knew mountain breathlessness long before: a Chinese text from about 30 BCE describes the “Big Headache Mountains”, and Arabia has high mountains too.
altitude-breath.gap.2: Some commentators read “climbing into the sky” as attempting the impossible, a common image for something one cannot do.
altitude-breath.media.0.cap: Mount Everest. At its summit the air has about a third of its sea-level pressure.
altitude-breath.media.1.cap: An old engraving of Pascal's Puy de Dôme experiment.
altitude-breath.media.2.cap: Paul Bert, who found that altitude sickness is caused by lack of oxygen.
green-fire.title: Fire From the Green Tree
green-fire.hook: “He made fire for you from the green tree.” Every burning log releases sunlight that green leaves once captured.
green-fire.science.0: In 1779 Jan Ingenhousz found that plants give off bubbles of oxygen from their green parts only in sunlight: the discovery of photosynthesis. Julius Robert Mayer then proposed that plants turn the energy of light into chemical energy.
green-fire.science.1: Leaves are green because of chlorophyll, which captures sunlight inside chloroplasts. With that energy, plants build sugars from carbon dioxide and water; Melvin Calvin traced the path of the carbon and won the 1961 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
green-fire.science.2: Wood is built from those sugars. When it burns, the stored energy of sunlight comes back out as heat and light. Photosynthesis around the world captures energy at about 130 terawatts, some eight times the power used by all of human civilisation.
green-fire.stats.0.label: Photosynthesis discovered (Ingenhousz)
green-fire.stats.1.label: Nobel Prize for the path of carbon (Calvin)
green-fire.stats.2.label: Power captured by photosynthesis worldwide
green-fire.proof.0.title: Ingenhousz: light is the key
green-fire.proof.0.text: At a country house near London, Jan Ingenhousz shows that plants under water give off bubbles from their green parts in sunlight, and stop in the shade.
green-fire.proof.1.title: Mayer: light into chemical energy
green-fire.proof.1.text: Julius Robert Mayer proposes that plants turn the energy of light into chemical energy.
green-fire.proof.2.title: Calvin: following the carbon
green-fire.proof.2.text: Melvin Calvin traces how plants turn carbon dioxide into sugar, step by step. He wins the 1961 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
green-fire.fit.0: The verse ties fire to the green tree, and the energy in burning wood was captured from sunlight by green leaves.
green-fire.fit.1: 56:71–72 asks who produced the tree behind your fire, pointing to the tree as the true source of the fire.
green-fire.gap.0: Classical commentators explain the verse by the markh and ʿafār trees, whose green branches Arabs rubbed together to make fire. The plain meaning was familiar.
green-fire.gap.1: Every wood fire comes from a tree, so the verse needs no hidden science to be true.
green-fire.gap.2: Chlorophyll, sugar and stored energy are not mentioned in the verses.
green-fire.media.0.cap: A green leaf: a solar panel that stores energy in wood.
green-fire.media.1.cap: Leaf cells packed with green chloroplasts, where sunlight is captured.
crow-burial.title: The Crow That Dug the Ground
crow-burial.hook: In the Quran, the first burial is taught by a crow scratching the ground. Crows turned out to be among the cleverest animals on Earth.
crow-burial.science.0: Crows, ravens and jays, the corvid family, are among the most intelligent animals known. In 1996 Gavin Hunt reported that wild New Caledonian crows make hooked tools from twigs and leaves. In 2002 a crow named Betty bent a straight wire into a hook to lift food out of a tube.
crow-burial.science.1: Corvids hide food in the ground and remember it. In 1998 Nicola Clayton and Anthony Dickinson showed that scrub jays remember what they hid, where, and how long ago. Wild American crows remember the faces of people who threatened them, and they gather around a dead crow to learn about danger.
crow-burial.stats.0.label: Crows making hooked tools (Hunt)
crow-burial.stats.1.label: Jays remember what, where and when
crow-burial.stats.2.label: Crows gather around their dead
crow-burial.disc.who: Hunt · Clayton & Dickinson · Weir & Kacelnik · Marzluff
crow-burial.proof.0.title: Tool makers
crow-burial.proof.0.text: Gavin Hunt describes wild New Caledonian crows making hooked tools from twigs and leaves (Nature 379, 249).
crow-burial.proof.1.title: Hidden food, remembered
crow-burial.proof.1.text: Nicola Clayton and Anthony Dickinson show that scrub jays remember what food they hid, where, and how long ago (Nature 395, 272).
crow-burial.proof.2.title: Betty bends a wire
crow-burial.proof.2.text: At Oxford, Alex Weir, Jackie Chappell and Alex Kacelnik watch a crow bend a straight wire into a hook to reach food (Science 297, 981).
crow-burial.proof.3.title: Crows at their dead
crow-burial.proof.3.text: Kaeli Swift and John Marzluff find that wild American crows gather around a dead crow, and afterwards avoid the place and the people linked to it (Animal Behaviour 109, 187).
crow-burial.fit.0: The verse shows a crow scratching the ground as a teacher. Crows do dig and hide things in the ground, and are skilled learners and problem-solvers.
crow-burial.fit.1: Crows react to their own dead, the very situation in the story.
crow-burial.gap.0: The verse tells a story about the sons of Adam. It does not claim that crows are intelligent.
crow-burial.gap.1: People have always seen crows digging and hiding food; that part was never hidden.
crow-burial.gap.2: Commentators say the crow in the story buried another dead crow. Wild crows have not been seen doing that, although they do gather around their dead.
crow-burial.media.0.cap: A New Caledonian crow, a species that makes its own tools.
